candidateRows: Theism provides a sounder foundation than atheism for objective moral values and duties.
This states Craig's two-part thesis and directly answers the debate's controlling question about the comparative grounding of objective morality.
After the moderator frames the dispute and introduces both participants, Craig begins by announcing the two contentions that organize his opening case.
God's necessarily good character grounds objective moral values, while commands consistent with that character constitute objective duties.
This supplies the positive metaphysical account at the heart of the pro side: divine nature explains value and divine commands explain obligation.
Craig develops his first contention by separating moral values from duties and assigning each a distinct but related foundation in God.
Godless normative realism is less plausible than theism because its commitment to independently real abstract moral objects is metaphysically extravagant and insufficiently supported.
The argument attacks the ontology required by the opposing account and presents comparative theoretical economy as a major reason to prefer theism.
Wielenberg's godless realist claim that objective moral features exist independently of God.
Having presented the positive theistic foundation, Craig turns to his first extended criticism of Wielenberg's alternative and its abstract ontology.
The proposed causal supervenience of abstract moral properties on physical situations is obscure, unexplained, and incompatible with the naturalistic aspirations of godless realism.
This challenges the mechanism connecting nonmoral reality to moral facts, a necessary explanatory bridge within the opposing account of objective morality.
Wielenberg's proposal that nonmoral physical features robustly cause corresponding moral properties to be instantiated.
Craig grants moral Platonism for argument's sake, then argues that its relation between physical situations and abstract moral properties remains unintelligible.
Defining obligation through decisive moral reasons mishandles supererogation, wrongly tends to require the best act, and yields only conditional rather than unconditional duties.
The move contests whether godless normative realism can account for genuine obligation, one of the two principal phenomena named in the motion.
Wielenberg's account identifying moral obligations with actions supported by decisive moral reasons.
After criticizing moral-property supervenience, Craig shifts from values to duties and tests Wielenberg's reasons-based theory against demanding and optional actions.
Causal closure and a non-enduring succession of mental states eliminate free agency, persistent moral agents, and therefore genuine accountability under godless normative realism.
This argues that the opposing worldview cannot preserve the agency and accountability required for objective moral duties to apply to persons.
Wielenberg's acceptance of physical causal closure and his account of the self as successive mental states.
Craig's next objection moves from the constitution of duties to the conditions for responsible action, claiming the opposing metaphysics dissolves moral agency.
Naturalism and evolution give a defeater for the reliability of moral beliefs, whereas theism can secure reliable cognitive faculties and moral knowledge.
The argument targets epistemic access to objective morality, claiming that the rival view undermines confidence in the very moral beliefs it affirms.
Wielenberg's naturalistic explanation of reliable moral belief and knowledge within godless normative realism.
Following objections about ontology and agency, Craig argues that evolutionary naturalism defeats trust in cognition generally and moral cognition specifically.
Moral features are irreducible fundamentals: suffering is intrinsically bad, and relevant situational features robustly cause obligations without dependence on God.
This presents the con side's positive account of objective value and duty and directly locates their sources in nondivine features of reality.
Wielenberg begins his opening with a shared moral example, distinguishes the competing explanations, and outlines his fundamentalist realist alternative.
Craig's objections from obscure causal relations and unexplained necessary connections have parallel force against theism, so they confer no comparative advantage.
The move supplies a general parity strategy and applies it to several of Craig's principal objections, challenging their ability to distinguish the views.
Craig's objections that godless realism posits obscure causation and unexplained necessary moral connections.
After stating his own account, Wielenberg argues that comparative evaluation must check whether each criticism has an equally serious theistic counterpart.
If unknown physical-to-nonphysical causal powers make godless realism 'voodoo metaphysics,' Craig's interactionist dualism is vulnerable to the same charge.
This concise symmetry argument rebuts a memorable criticism of the rival ontology and reinforces the broader claim that Craig's objections cancel out.
Craig's charge that unknown causal powers attributed to physical objects amount to voodoo metaphysics.
Wielenberg follows his general parity argument with a focused response to Craig's rhetoric about causal powers unknown to contemporary physics.
Causal closure does not entail that mental states lack physical effects unless one adds the contentious premise that mental states cannot also be physical states.
The argument directly answers the claim that godless normative realism undermines agency, freedom, moral knowledge, and therefore the intelligibility of obligation.
Craig's claim that causal closure renders mental states causally ineffective and undermines the self, freedom, and moral knowledge.

Wielenberg argues that causal closure supplies a complete physical cause but does not exclude mental causation if some mental states are physical, while noting parallel interaction problems for Craig's dualism.

Craig has not shown an advantage concerning supererogation because Christian commands may make his examples obligatory, while exclusionary permissions can accommodate such acts within Wielenberg's view.
Whether godless normative realism can distinguish duty from action beyond duty is a direct test of its proposed account of objective moral reasons and obligations.
Craig's objection that Wielenberg's reasons-based account cannot accommodate morally supererogatory actions.

Wielenberg first questions whether Christian love commands permit Craig's examples to exceed duty, then invokes Razian exclusionary permission to explain when decisive reasons need not generate an obligation.
Divine commands are not the uniquely possible ground of obligations, because suffering, promises, and other morally relevant features can themselves generate genuine duties.
This challenges the central divine-command thesis and positively contrasts it with godless normative realism's plural grounding of objective moral obligations.
Craig's foundational contention that only God's commands can ultimately generate unconditional and genuine moral obligations.
Using a rescue case and an analogy with a promise-only theory, Wielenberg argues that restricting duty generation to one feature conflicts with common moral judgment and favors a pluralist account.
Commands bind only agents who apprehend both their content and the commander's authority, so divine-command theory implausibly leaves unaware nonbelievers without obligations.
The move alleges that Craig's grounding theory fails to extend objective duties to a substantial class of moral agents, threatening its universality.
Craig's account of human obligations as constituted by authoritative divine commands issued to humanity.

Wielenberg uses parental commands, anonymous notes, and an unreceived instruction to argue that unknown authority cannot impose a duty, distinguishing lack of obligation from mere lack of moral knowledge.
Divine-command theory makes actual wrongdoing difficult to explain because an omniscient God would pointlessly worsen foreknown disobedience by issuing commands that cannot alter conduct.
The argument attacks the theory's explanation of wrong action itself, alleging tension between divine omniscience, command issuance, and the occurrence of violated obligations.
Craig's claim that divine commands explain what constitutes morally wrong conduct and violations of objective obligation.
In the child-rescue case, Wielenberg reasons that a futile command adds the evil of obligation violation without preventing the foreknown act, making selective effective commands seem preferable.

Divine commands can be the ultimate source within a hierarchy whose derivative principles govern particular cases, so the theory neither requires case-specific commands nor arbitrarily excludes lower sources.
The response clarifies the core theistic grounding thesis and directly addresses the alleged arbitrariness on which Wielenberg's first major challenge depends.
Wielenberg's objection that Craig arbitrarily treats divine commands as the only morally relevant source capable of generating obligations.

Craig distinguishes ultimate grounding from derivative moral facts: general divine commands ground a hierarchy, while agents apply principles involving promises and other facts in specific circumstances.
Nonbelievers can remain obligated because people intuitively grasp the content and authority of God's moral law even when they do not identify its source as God.
This reply defends the universal applicability of divine commands against the claim that theistic grounding deprives nonbelievers of all moral obligations.
Wielenberg's contention that people unaware of God's commands or authority cannot be bound by them and therefore lack obligations.
Craig says moral law is intuitively apprehended and compares it to recognizing an authoritative no-trespassing prohibition without knowing who posted the sign.
General divine commands make retributive responsibility possible, while Wielenberg's foreknowledge objection imports a disputed middle-knowledge doctrine not required by divine-command theory.
The response seeks to preserve the divine-command explanation of wrongdoing by denying a required foreknowledge premise and supplying a reason for general commands.
Wielenberg's argument that God inexplicably commands foreknown disobedience and thereby introduces additional evil into the world.
Craig distinguishes divine-command theory from middle knowledge and argues that general commands establish culpability, retributive justice, and divine judgment for evil actions.

Godless normative realism remains less plausible because its abstract moral ontology is extravagant and its accounts of moral causation, supererogation, freedom, and moral knowledge face unresolved objections.
This extended move supplies Craig's main comparative case that the atheistic account offers a weaker foundation for objective values and duties than theism.
Wielenberg's strategy of answering objections to godless normative realism by alleging parallel obscurities and difficulties for theism.

Craig argues that parity replies leave original problems unresolved, contrasts abstract Platonism with a concrete God, defends soul-body causation, and renews objections involving supererogation, physical closure, freedom, and evolutionary reliability.

Craig's objections do not establish a comparative advantage, while divine-command theory still faces counterexamples involving psychopaths, the rationale for commands, and the moral force of suffering independently of God.
The move is Wielenberg's comprehensive defense of godless normative realism and his final comparative argument that Craig's account cannot adequately explain objective morality.
Craig's preceding defense of theism and renewed objections concerning metaphysical obscurity, freedom, moral knowledge, and supererogation.

Wielenberg argues that shared obscurities do not favor Craig, disputes claims about physical minds and evolutionary unreliability, and presses psychopath, wrong-action, and extreme-suffering cases against divine-command grounding.
The child-in-flames case reveals an experienced moral obligation but cannot establish that the obligation is ultimately grounded independently of God.
This directly defends the theistic account against a central counterexample intended to show that morally urgent circumstances generate duties without divine commands.
Wielenberg’s claim that the child-in-flames case demonstrates obligations whose ultimate ground is independent of God.
Craig distinguishes immediate awareness of an objective obligation from knowledge of its ultimate source, arguing that experience supports the former without settling the latter.
The distinction between evil grounded in God’s being and wrongness grounded in divine commands avoids the alleged circularity in explaining accountability.
The move protects the value-duty distinction at the heart of Craig’s theory and answers the claim that his explanation of wrong action is viciously circular.
Wielenberg’s accusation that Craig circularly invokes wrong acts to explain why divine commands are needed to make acts wrong.
Craig says he appealed to pre-command evil rather than pre-command wrongness, with goodness and evil grounded in God’s being and duties arising from commands.
Godless normative realism remains metaphysically extravagant because its additional realm of abstract moral objects has not received a supporting argument.
The move directly compares the ontological plausibility of the rival foundations and challenges the affirmative case for godless normative realism itself.
Wielenberg’s defense of godless normative realism despite Craig’s objection that its abstract moral ontology is extravagant.
Craig argues that adding abstract moral objects beyond concrete reality, physical cosmology, and biological evolution is a substantial commitment requiring justification that was not supplied.
Wielenberg’s proposed connection between physical situations and abstract moral properties is unintelligible because abstract objects appear causally inert.
This attacks the explanatory mechanism by which godless normative realism connects concrete circumstances to abstract moral properties, a core grounding problem in the debate.
Wielenberg’s contention that a causal relation can explain how abstract moral properties are connected with physical situations.
Craig says the problem is not merely the absence of a detailed causal theory but the apparent nonexistence of causal commerce between physical and abstract objects.
Reducing mental states to brain states eliminates the causal agency and freedom required for genuine moral obligation.
The argument challenges whether Wielenberg’s naturalistic framework can preserve free agency, which Craig treats as a necessary condition of morally binding duties.
Wielenberg’s defense of reducing mental states to physical brain states while retaining the freedom needed for moral responsibility.
Craig argues that mental and brain states have different properties and that physical determination leaves mental states unable to originate actions, thereby undermining free will and obligation.
Naturalism combined with unguided evolution undercuts confidence in reliable cognition because selection favors adaptive behavior rather than true belief.
This is Craig’s principal epistemic objection to godless normative realism, alleging that its naturalistic setting defeats both general and specifically moral knowledge.
Wielenberg’s claim that the observed reliability of evolved believers answers Plantinga’s evolutionary argument against naturalism.
Craig maintains that appealing to evolution’s actual production of reliable believers assumes the reliability at issue and that reliable cognition would instead count against unguided naturalism.
Observed cognitive reliability can justify belief in reliable evolved faculties despite speculative arguments that unguided evolution probably produces unreliable cognition.
The move answers the main epistemic challenge to moral knowledge under naturalism and therefore protects Wielenberg’s ability to claim knowledge of objective moral facts.
Craig’s Plantinga-based argument that naturalism and unguided evolution make reliable cognition, including moral knowledge, improbable.
Using a repeatedly successful lighter as an analogy, Wielenberg argues that reasonable acceptance of naturalism and observed reliability are not overturned by an armchair probability argument.
The capacity to prevent immense suffering can itself generate a duty, making a theory that additionally requires a divine order deeply implausible.
The argument presents the debate’s central intuitive test of whether duties require divine commands or can arise from morally salient nondivine facts themselves.
Craig’s response that experience of an urgent obligation cannot reveal whether its ultimate source is a divine command.
Wielenberg emphasizes that Craig did not reject the implication that preventing vast suffering is insufficient by itself and portrays the required divine order as implausible.
Craig’s treatment of psychopaths implies both that they lack obligations because they cannot grasp moral authority and that they possess obligations as culpable evildoers.
This alleges an internal contradiction in the theistic account’s explanation of how divine commands bind nonbelievers and secure universal accountability for evil acts.
Craig’s claim that psychopaths lacking moral knowledge may be nonculpable while divine commands nevertheless hold evildoers universally accountable.

Wielenberg combines psychopaths’ inability to grasp moral authority with Craig’s insistence that general commands prevent evildoers from acting with impunity, deriving opposing conclusions about obligation.
Godless normative realism is supported abductively as the best available explanation of objective moral facts after rival accounts are comparatively ruled out.
This supplies the positive argumentative structure for Wielenberg’s view, answering the recurring demand for justification of its entities and explaining how debate against rivals contributes.
Wielenberg characterizes his position as an inference to the best explanation: objective moral facts need an account, rival theories must be excluded, and normative entities best explain them.
Divine commands ground duties rather than values, while God's nature grounds moral value and his commands disclose humanity's evil condition and need for reconciliation.
The move clarifies the theory's fundamental value-duty distinction and supplies Craig's explanation for why God issues commands despite foreknown disobedience.
The question and Wielenberg's earlier challenge concerning evil acts, wrong acts, and apparently unnecessary divine commands.
After a question conflates evil with wrongness absent divine commands, Craig distinguishes values from duties and explains divine law as serving humanity's recognition, repentance, and salvation.
If goodness and evil already exist without divine commands, God could merely inform people of those values, leaving the necessity of commands unexplained.
This directly renews the challenge to divine-command necessity by arguing that moral information could achieve the stated benefit without creating additional obligations.
Craig's claim that God gives commands for humanity's good, repentance, reception of grace, and eventual communion with God.
Wielenberg accepts for discussion Craig's distinction between value and obligation, then argues that communicating knowledge of good and evil would suffice without commands.
Divine-command theory may treat the constitution of obligations by God's commands as an explanatory ultimate, or explain obedience through God's self-inclusive command to obey all his commands.
The answer addresses whether divine-command theory can ground the normative requirement to obey God without an illicit regress or vicious circularity.
The question whether divine-command theory can explain why anyone should obey God's commands and where that normative requirement is grounded.
Craig offers two answers: constitution by command can terminate explanation legitimately, and a universal command to obey God's commands can include itself without vicious circularity.
Every objective moral theory ultimately relies on unexplained moral axioms, so theism and atheism differ over which axioms they accept rather than whether they have foundations.
This is a core parity argument for godless normative realism, denying that theism enjoys a unique explanatory advantage over atheistic moral realism.
Craig's proposed explanations of why divine commands obligate and the broader theistic claim to provide a superior moral foundation.
Wielenberg argues that both positions terminate in moral axioms and invokes prominent divine-command theorists' reliance on brute normative reasons for obedience.
Obscurity about how natural properties produce obligations is not fatal to godless realism because all causal theories eventually reach relations with no deeper mechanism, including Craig's view.
The move defends the metaphysical making relation at the heart of Wielenberg's account and argues that Craig's obscurity objection applies symmetrically to causal explanation generally.
Craig's objection that causation between natural features and abstract moral properties is obscure and lacks an intelligible mechanism.
Asked whether grounding would improve his view, Wielenberg defends causation by comparing its unexplained endpoint with ordinary physical and mind-body causal relations.
Wielenberg's appeal to unexplained causation undermines his position because mind-body causation is experientially known to occur, whereas no comparable basis establishes natural-to-moral causation.
This sharpens Craig's obscurity objection by distinguishing ignorance of a known mechanism from lacking grounds to believe the proposed cross-category causal relation occurs at all.
Wielenberg's contention that unexplained causal connections are unavoidable and therefore cannot be a fatal objection to his moral realism.
Craig concedes that mechanisms can remain unknown but argues that Wielenberg lacks the independent experiential warrant available for mind-body interaction or a demonstrably effective drug.
Craig's treatment of psychopathy fails because impaired grasp of morality appears to remove obligations on his account, while his principles also require psychopaths to remain accountable for evil.
The objection tests the internal consistency and scope of Craig's account of moral obligation by applying it to agents with atypical moral understanding.
Craig's conditional appeal to legal culpability, moral knowledge, and psychopathy as a mental disorder when assessing psychopaths' obligations.

After distinguishing empirical research from Craig's anecdotal example, Wielenberg argues that legal responsibility does not resolve whether psychopaths possess obligations under Craig's own principles.
God's essential goodness follows from the concept of God as the greatest conceivable and worship-worthy being, whose nature is itself the paradigm and metric of moral goodness.
The move states Craig's foundational account of moral value and answers the central challenge of how God's goodness can be assessed without an external standard.
The question asking what metric can establish that God is genuinely good if God is also used to define and understand goodness.
Craig invokes the greatest-conceivable-being concept, worthiness of worship, and a paradigm analogy to present God's essentially loving nature as the standard of goodness.
Calling God worthy of worship embeds an unexplained normative claim in theistic reality, so theism cannot avoid the same brute moral axioms it attributes to godless realism.
This directly challenges the claimed explanatory superiority of theistic grounding by locating an irreducible normative premise within Craig's own definition of God.
Craig's claim that God is by definition worthy of worship and therefore serves as the self-explanatory paradigm and metric of goodness.
Wielenberg notes that worthiness is already normative and argues that a worship-worthy unexplained God leaves the theist with brute normativity just as the atheist has it.
Brute moral axioms are justified by their comparative plausibility, while irreducible moral entities are warranted as part of the best explanation of objective moral facts.
The answer supplies Wielenberg's positive epistemic and abductive defense of godless normative realism and frames the debate as a comparison between rival explanatory accounts.
The question demanding arguments or evidence for the brute moral facts and abstract moral entities posited by Wielenberg's realist account.
Wielenberg concedes that basic axioms rest on seeming plausible, argues Craig likewise selects foundational axioms, and defends moral Platonism by inference to the best explanation.
